newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM predicts long standoff in Lima crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM predicts long standoff in Lima crisis.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto predicted on Tuesday that the Lima hostage crisis would be a drawn-out affair and cancelled an important visit by his foreign minister to South Korea.
But Hashimoto said the prospect of a prolonged standoff at the Japanese ambassador's residence meant there would be no "get-tough" actions to resolve the week-old crisis.
"I think it will take time (to resolve the crisis)," Hashimoto told reporters shortly after speaking by telephone to Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori.
"The fact that it will take time means that no get-tough approach will be taken," Hashimoto said.
Speaking earlier to reporters, Hashimoto said the crisis would be "prolonged".
"Taking a long time means that the Peruvian government will not resort to forceful measures," he said. "We are braced for a long haul, even if the New Year holiday is ruined."
The prime minister said the Peruvian government and the guerrillas holding around 140 hostages at Ambassador Morihisa Aoki's residence were in contact with each other to work out a solution.
"The channel of negotiations set with the terrorist group is working properly," Hashimoto said.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas, who stormed the ambassador's home last Tuesday during a reception in honour of Emperor Akihito's birthday, want the release of 400 imprisoned comrades in exchange for the hostages. President Alberto Fujimori has said no serious negotiations can start until the rebels lay down their arms and unconditionally release all their remaining captives.

Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, announcing he was cancelling a planned visit to South Korea later this week after consulting Hashimoto, said "difficult judgments" were needed on how to end the hostage crisis.
"After consulting Prime Minister (Ryutaro) Hashimoto and the South Korean government, I decided to cancel my visit scheduled for December 26 and 27," Ikeda told a news conference.
"We are entering a stage which requires us to make difficult judgments," Ikeda said. "We will seek the release of the remaining hostages as soon as possible."
Ikeda spent four days in Lima as Japan's on-the-spot adviser and returned to Tokyo on Monday evening.

The foreign minister had planned to hold talks with his South Korean counterpart Yoo Chong-ha ahead of a summit meeting in Japan in late January between Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.

Ikeda said he did not even rule out the possibility that the hostage crisis could force the cancellation of the summit, due to he held in the resort city of Beppu on Japan's southernmost main island of Kyushu on January 25 and 26.
"It all hinges on the developments in the incident in Peru," Ikeda said.

In a report from Lima, Japan's Kyodo news agency said the Japanese task force dealing with the situation there believed the rebels next move would be to release more captives, reducing the number of hostages to around 40.

"The task force, headed by Japanese Ambassador to Mexico Terusuke Terada, has begun preparing for the further release of diplomats, including Japanese, out of the remaining captives," Kyodo said, quoting unnamed Japanese sources.
